items.title: Antarctica is governed by an international treaty

options.text: It is divided into national territories
The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze territorial claims, demilitarised the continent and committed it to scientific cooperation; 56 countries are now parties
It is divided between Argentina and Chile

items.reveal:
The original 12 signatories (1959) included the US, USSR, UK, Australia, France, Argentina and Chile. The treaty entered force in 1961. The Protocol on Environmental Protection (Madrid Protocol, 1991, in force 1998) prohibits mineral extraction.

Seven countries maintain dormant territorial claims (UK, Norway, France, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, Chile). The US and Russia reserve the right to claim. Treaty parties operate around 70 year-round research stations.

The treaty is one of the most successful international agreements of the Cold War era — both superpowers wanted the demilitarisation to apply to the other.
items.why: Some territory remains explicitly outside the state system. Antarctica's governance shows what's possible when no major power has a strong sovereignty claim — but also illustrates how fragile such arrangements may be as resource interests grow.

items.title: Stratified sampling deliberately includes defined subgroups
items.claim: Why use stratified sampling rather than random?

options.text: Stratified sampling deliberately includes proportions from defined subgroups (e.g. age categories in a questionnaire, river sections by gradient), reducing the risk of missing minority categories

items.reveal:
Sampling types: random (every member equally likely), systematic (every nth member — e.g. every 10 m along a river transect), stratified (proportional samples from defined groups), opportunistic (whoever is available — least rigorous).

GCSE and A-level NEA fieldwork requires explicit justification of sampling strategy. Small samples (n<30) limit statistical analysis; subgroup analysis needs larger samples in each stratum.

Fieldwork ethics — informed consent for questionnaires, minimising impact on study sites — has become more prominent in awarding-body specifications.
items.why: Bad sampling produces bad results regardless of subsequent analysis. Sampling design is upstream of every statistical inference — and is the most common point of failure in student fieldwork.

items.title: Scotland is still rising — southern England is sinking
items.claim: What is glacial isostatic adjustment in the British Isles?

options.text: Britain has fully recovered from the Ice Age

Scotland and northern England rise by 1-2 mm/year as crust rebounds from glacial loading; southern and eastern England subside by around 1 mm/year as the forebulge collapses — both measured directly by GPS
The motion is too slow to measure

items.reveal:
When the British-Irish Ice Sheet melted (around 10,000 years ago), the depressed crust began to rebound. Because the mantle behaves viscously over thousand-year timescales, the response is still ongoing.

The British Isles GNSS Facility (BIGF) measures vertical motion directly. Net result for relative sea level: southern England experiences faster sea-level rise than would be expected from climate alone, while northern Scotland experiences slower (or in some places falling) relative sea level.

Fenno-Scandinavia is rebounding even faster — up to 10 mm/year in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia. The Baltic Sea is gradually shrinking on the Scandinavian side.
items.why: Sea-level projections combine global climate signal with local geophysics. The Thames Barrier defends a coast that is itself sinking — accelerating the apparent rise.
